items.t: Conditions likely to benefit from short- or long-term glucocorticoid therapy, e.g. severe allergy and asthma, collagen and rheumatic disorders, severe skin disease, inflammatory bowel disease, sarcoidosis, blood disorders, leukaemia/lymphoma, nephrotic syndrome.

src.q: Prednisolone is indicated in the management of all conditions deemed likely to benefit from short- or long-term glucocorticoid therapy.
Some of the principal indications are: bronchial asthma, severe hypersensitivity reactions, anaphylaxis; rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK SmPCs (5 mg tablets, 20 mg tablets, 10 mg/mL oral solution) or SPS pages accessed.

items.t: Adults: lowest effective dose for the shortest time. Initial dose 5-60 mg daily depending on the condition (divided doses usually used); reduce gradually to the lowest maintenance dose.

src.q: The lowest effective dose should be used for the minimum period in order to minimise side effects.
The initial dosage of Prednisolone Tablets may vary from 5mg to 60mg or more depending on the disorder being treated.

items.t: Guide doses: allergic and skin disorders 5-15 mg daily; collagenosis 20-30 mg daily; rheumatoid arthritis 10-15 mg daily initially (oral solution SmPC: 7.5-10 mg daily); blood disorders and lymphoma 15-60 mg daily.

src.q: Allergic and skin disorders : Initial doses of 5-15 mg daily are commonly adequate. Collagenosis : Initial doses of 20-30 mg daily are frequently effective.
Rheumatoid arthritis : The usual initial dose is 10-15 mg daily.
Blood disorders and lymphoma : An initial daily dose of 15-60 mg is often necessary
Rheumatoid arthritis: 7.5mg (0.75ml) to 10mg (1ml) daily.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC, short-term treatment: 20-30 mg daily for the first few days, then reduce by 2.5-5 mg every 2-5 days. Most other conditions: 10-100 mg daily for 1-3 weeks, then reduce to the minimum effective dose.

src.q: Short-term treatment: 20mg (2ml) to 30mg (3ml) daily for the first few days, subsequently reducing the daily dosage by 2.5mg (0.25ml) or 5mg (0.5ml) every two to five days
Most other conditions: 10mg (1ml) to 100mg (10ml) daily for one to three weeks, then reducing to the minimum effective dosage.

items.t: Withdrawal: after more than about 7.5 mg daily for over 3 weeks, do not stop abruptly. Courses of up to 40 mg daily for up to 3 weeks can usually be stopped abruptly if relapse is unlikely, except in at-risk groups (repeated courses, recent long-term therapy, other causes of adrenal insufficiency, more than 40 mg daily, evening doses).

src.q: In patients who have received more than physiological dose for systemic corticosteroids (approximately 7.5mg prednisolone or equivalent) for greater than 3 weeks, withdrawal should not be abrupt.
Abrupt withdrawal of doses of up to 40mg daily of prednisolone, or equivalent for 3 weeks is unlikely to lead to clinically relevant HPA-axis suppression, in the majority of patients.

items.t: During prolonged therapy, intercurrent illness, trauma or surgery need a temporary dose increase.

src.q: During prolonged therapy any intercurrent illness, trauma or surgical procedure will require a temporary increase in dosage

items.t: Use only when specifically indicated, at the minimum dose for the shortest time; alternate-day dosing preferred. Fractions of the adult dose may be used (e.g. 75% at 12 years, 50% at 7 years, 25% at 1 year).

src.q: Prednisolone should be used only when specifically indicated, in a minimum dosage and for the shortest possible time.
Fractions of the adult dosage may be used (e.g. 75% at 12 years, 50% at 7 years and 25% at 1 year)

items.t: Acute asthma (oral solution SmPC): over 5 years 30-40 mg; 2-5 years 20 mg; under 2 years (hospital) 10 mg, for up to 3 days; no taper needed.

src.q: For children over 5 years use a dose of 30-40mg (3-4ml) prednisolone. For children aged 2-5 years use a dose of 20mg (2ml) prednisolone.
at a dose of 10mg (1ml) for up to three days
There is no need to taper the dose at the end of treatment.

items.t: Acute asthma in children already on maintenance steroid tablets: 2 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg.

src.q: Those already receiving maintenance steroid tablets should receive 2mg/kg prednisolone up to a maximum dose of 60mg (6ml).

items.t: Steroids cause growth retardation, which may be irreversible: avoid long-term pharmacological doses; monitor growth.

src.q: Corticosteroids cause growth retardation in infancy, childhood and adolescence, which may be irreversible and therefore long-term administration of pharmacological doses should be avoided.

items.t: All UK SmPCs: hypersensitivity to prednisolone or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1. Systemic infections unless specific anti-infective therapy is employed.

items.t: 5 mg tablet and oral solution SmPCs: systemic infection unless specific anti-infective treatment is given. 5 mg tablet SmPC: ocular herpes simplex (risk of perforation).

src.q: Patients with ocular herpes simplex due to the possibility of perforation.
Systemic infections, unless specific anti-infective therapy is employed. Live virus immunisation.

items.t: Oral solution SmPC: live virus immunisation. 20 mg tablet SPC: systemic fungal infection; live vaccines in patients on immunosuppressive doses. The 20 mg SPC adds that in life-saving situations the contraindications generally do not apply.

src.q: Systemic fungal infection. Administration of live vaccines is contraindicated in patients receiving corticosteroids in immunosuppressive doses.
In those conditions when treatment with prednisolone can save lives, none of the contraindications generally apply.

items.t: Caution and frequent monitoring in: diabetes (or family history), glaucoma (or family history), hypertension or heart failure, liver failure, epilepsy, osteoporosis, severe affective disorder or previous steroid psychosis, peptic ulcer, previous steroid myopathy, thromboembolic disorders, renal insufficiency, tuberculosis history, recent myocardial infarction.

src.q: Caution is necessary when corticosteroids, including prednisolone, are prescribed to patients with the following conditions and frequent patient monitoring is necessary: Diabetes mellitus or in those with a family history of diabetes.
Peptic ulceration. Previous steroid myopathy.
Renal insufficiency. Tuberculosis: Those with a history of, or X-ray changes characteristic of tuberculosis.

items.t: Psychiatric reactions (mood change, depression, suicidal thoughts, psychosis) are common and usually start within days or weeks; patients/carers should seek advice if worrying symptoms occur. Particular care with a personal or first-degree family history of severe affective disorder.

src.q: Patients/carers should be encouraged to seek medical advice if worrying psychological symptoms develop, especially if depressed mood or suicidal ideation is suspected.

Particular care is required when considering the use of systemic corticosteroids in patients with existing or previous history of severe affective disorders in themselves or in their first degree relatives.

items.t: Infections may be masked. Chickenpox and measles can be severe or fatal: non-immune exposed patients need urgent advice (VZIG within 10 days for chickenpox exposure). Do not stop steroids if chickenpox develops.

src.q: Chickenpox is of particular concern since this normally minor illness may be fatal in immunosuppressed patients.
this should be given within 10 days of exposure to chickenpox
Corticosteroids should not be stopped and the dose may need to be increased.

items.t: Systemic sclerosis: increased risk of scleroderma renal crisis at 15 mg/day or more; check blood pressure and serum creatinine routinely.

src.q: Caution is required in patients with systemic sclerosis because of an increased incidence of (possibly fatal) scleroderma renal crisis with hypertension and decreased urinary output observed with a daily dose of 15 mg or more prednisolone.

items.t: Myasthenia gravis on anticholinesterases: use cautiously. Hypothyroidism or chronic liver disease: effect may be enhanced. Phaeochromocytoma (20 mg SPC): only after risk/benefit evaluation.

src.q: Glucocorticoids should be used cautiously in patients with myasthenia gravis receiving anticholinesterase therapy.
The effect of corticosteroids may be enhanced in patients with hypothyroidism in those with chronic liver disease with impaired hepatic function.
Corticosteroids should only be administered to patients with suspected or identified pheochromocytoma following consideration of individual risk/benefit.

items.t: Blurred vision or visual disturbance: consider ophthalmology referral (cataract, glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy). Elderly: closer supervision.

src.q: If a patient presents with symptoms such as blurred vision or other visual disturbances, the patient should be considered for referral to an ophthalmologist
Close clinical supervision is required to avoid life threatening reactions.

items.t: Tablets contain lactose: not for galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: CYP3A inhibitors (including cobicistat): avoid unless benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic steroid effects; if used, monitor.

src.q: The combination should be avoided unless the benefit outweighs the increased risk of systemic corticosteroid side-effects, in which case patients should be monitored for systemic corticosteroid side-effects.

items.t: Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, rifampicin, rifabutin) reduce prednisolone effect; dose may need increasing.

src.q: Lack of expected response may be observed and dosage of prednisolone tablets may need to be increased.

items.t: NSAIDs and aspirin: higher risk of GI ulceration and bleeding. Use salicylates with caution; steroid withdrawal may cause salicylate toxicity.

src.q: Concomitant use of aspirin and Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) with corticosteroids increases the risk of gastro-intestinal bleeding and ulceration.
Salicylates and corticosteroids should be used concurrently with caution.

items.t: Anticoagulants (warfarin): effect may be reduced or enhanced; monitor INR closely.

src.q: Response to anticoagulants may be reduced or less often, enhanced by corticosteroids. Close monitoring of the INR or prothrombin time is required to avoid spontaneous bleeding.

items.t: Antidiabetic medicines (including insulin): steroids raise blood glucose; antidiabetic dose may need adjusting.

src.q: Patients with diabetes mellitus receiving concurrent insulin and/or oral hypoglycemic agents may require dosage adjustments of such therapy.

items.t: Potassium-lowering drugs (thiazides, loop diuretics, beta2-agonists at high doses, theophylline, amphotericin): more hypokalaemia; 20 mg SPC: monitor serum potassium closely.

src.q: Serum potassium should be closely monitored in patients receiving glucocorticoids and potassium reducing agents.
Increased risk of hypokalaemia if high doses of corticosteroids given with high doses of bambuterol, fenoteral, formoteral, ritodrine, salbutamol, salmeterol and terbutaline.

items.t: Antihypertensives and diuretics: their effects are antagonised. Methotrexate: increased risk of haematological toxicity. Ciclosporin raises prednisolone levels. Live vaccines: see contraindications.

src.q: The desired effects of hypoglycaemic agents (including insulin), antihypertensives and diuretics are antagonised by corticosteroids
Cytotoxics: Increased risk of haematological toxicity with methotrexate.

items.t: No dose adjustment stated. Use with caution in renal insufficiency (fluid retention); monitor frequently.

src.q: Because of the possibility of fluid retention, care must be taken when corticosteroids are administered to patients with renal insufficiency or hypertension or congestive heart failure.
Corticosteroids should be used with caution in patients with renal insufficiency.

items.t: Liver failure: blood levels may rise; caution and frequent monitoring. Chronic liver disease or cirrhosis: effect enhanced.

src.q: In patients with liver failure, blood levels of corticosteroid may be increased, as with other drugs which are metabolised in the liver. Frequent patient monitoring is therefore necessary.
Patients with hypothyroidism or liver cirrhosis will have an enhanced effect of corticosteroids.

items.t: SmPC: prescribe only when benefits outweigh risks; 88% of prednisolone is inactivated crossing the placenta. Prolonged or repeated use may increase the risk of intra-uterine growth restriction. Monitor pre-eclampsia or fluid retention closely.

src.q: As with all drugs, corticosteroids should only be prescribed when the benefits to the mother and child outweigh the risks.
88% of prednisolone is inactivated as it crosses the placenta
Patients with pre-eclampsia or fluid retention require close monitoring.

items.t: BUMPS: systemic corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; usually among the safest options for rheumatic and autoimmune disease. Some studies link early use with cleft lip/palate.

src.q: Systemic corticosteroids can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
Corticosteroid use in early pregnancy has been linked in some (but not all) studies to a higher chance of having a baby with a cleft lip and/or palate.

items.t: SmPC: up to 40 mg daily unlikely to affect the infant; at 40 mg or more monitor the infant for adrenal suppression. SPS: prednisolone is a preferred corticosteroid in breastfeeding; use lowest dose and duration.

src.q: Infants of mothers receiving 40mg or more daily should be monitored for signs of adrenal suppression
